 RBI Study Shows Loan Mix Helped Lower Average Bank Lending Rates During 2025–26 Easing
 The average rate on new bank loans fell 93 basis points between February 2025 and March 2026. RBI researchers estimate that 80 basis points came from changes in the rates banks charged, while 13 came from shifts in the mix of loans.
 SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth | SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure 
 Reserve Bank of India RBI 
 Key Details
 The RBI October 2026 Bulletin article Transmission to Lending Rates of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs): Price versus Composition Effects in WALR separates two reasons an average lending rate can move: banks changing loan rates and banks making different kinds of loans .  A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. The article also tests alternative ways of separating the effects; the precise split can vary with the method. 
 A Falling Average Rate Does Not Mean Every Loan Became Cheaper
 The weighted average lending rate (WALR) reflects both the interest rates banks charge and the amounts lent at each rate. It can therefore fall because banks reduce rates on comparable loans — or because a larger share of new lending goes to lower-rate borrowers, sectors or banks.
 During the easing period studied, the average rate on fresh loans fell 93 basis points . The researchers attribute most of that decline —  80 basis points  — to changes in lending rates. The remaining 13 basis points came from changes in where new credit flowed. Loan-mix effects also partly offset the rise in the average rate during the earlier tightening period.

 -Advertisement- 
 Loan-Mix Changes Can Obscure Policy Transmission
 Earlier RBI assessments have tracked how changes in the policy repo rate reach bank lending rates. This article adds a more precise reading of that transmission: a change in the average fresh-loan rate is not, by itself, a measure of how much banks repriced loans .
 That distinction is particularly useful for fresh lending, whose composition can change quickly. The researchers examine rates and loan amounts across banks and sectors, then test their results using several decomposition methods. The broad finding holds: both repricing and credit allocation shape the reported average . The analysis ends in March 2026; it does not assess transmission of the RBI’s October 2026 rate increase.
 Policy Relevance
 The finding changes how policymakers should read a familiar indicator, not how banks are required to price loans. Tracking rate and loan-mix effects separately would make it easier to see whether a policy change is reaching borrowers through repricing, or whether the aggregate number is being moved partly by shifts in credit. Sector-level results could also show where borrowing conditions differ from the system-wide average.
